# Brightest stars of the night sky — provenance report

<!-- Generated from authored/brightest-stars.json by scripts/authored_decks.py. Do not edit: change the dossier and rebuild. -->

**Deck:** [`decks/brightest-stars.ttl`](../decks/brightest-stars.ttl) · **Cards:** 52 · **Licence:** [CC BY 4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/) · **Compiled by:** Anton Wiklund · **Created:** 2026-10-04

52 cards on the brightest stars of the night sky. 49 cover every star with a name approved by the International Astronomical Union (IAU) that is brighter than apparent magnitude 2.0 (close pairs by their combined light), plus Polaris: front, the star's name, e.g. “Sirius”; back, its constellation, in English by its official IAU name (e.g. “Canis Major”), in Swedish by its Swedish name (“Stora hunden”), with the Bayer designation in a note. Three more ask for the brightest and second-brightest star of the night sky and the north pole star. Names from the IAU Working Group on Star Names; constellations and magnitudes from Wikidata, checked against SIMBAD.

## Licensing

The deck is licensed CC BY 4.0. The IAU star names and the decision which stars have one come from the IAU Working Group on Star Names' catalogue in its plain-text edition, which states that “All IAU-produced products (Images, Videos, Texts) are released under Creative Commons Attribution”, and the IAU releases the web texts of iau.org under CC BY 4.0; the official Latin names and genitives of the constellations come from the IAU's page “The Constellations”, also under CC BY 4.0. Using these as content sources was a deliberate choice: Wikidata (CC0) has no property that marks a name as IAU-approved, so the IAU list is needed to select the stars, and CC BY 4.0 lets anyone reuse the deck, commercially too, with attribution. The IAU is credited, by name, in the deck description, in the deck metadata (prov:wasDerivedFrom with title, creator and licence) and in this report, and nothing in the deck states or implies IAU endorsement. The WGSN file asks users to cite the official IAU version at https://www.iau.org/public/themes/naming_stars/, which now answers 404; the deck credits the WGSN's file and names the current IAU catalogue on exopla.net, which the IAU's 2026 announcement links as the IAU Star Names Catalog, as the official version. Wikidata (CC0) supplied the constellation of each star, the magnitudes used for the ranking and the Swedish names, with no conditions. The current catalogue on exopla.net (© the WGSN, no licence stated), SIMBAD (CDS; the service is offered under the ODbL, a share-alike database licence), astropy (BSD 3-clause; used only to compute constellations and Polaris's distance from the pole) and the Swedish Wikipedia (CC BY-SA 4.0) were used only to verify facts: no wording, list or selection was taken from them. The fronts of the superlative cards and all notes are the compiler's own wording.

## Method

1. Who did the work: Anton Wiklund compiled this deck with the help of AI agents (Claude, by Anthropic), which did the research, drafting and cross-checking at his direction. The cards were checked by machine (SIMBAD, astropy, live Wikidata and the app's SHACL and DCAT-AP validators) and in independent review rounds by further Claude agents, each logged under Quality control with its findings and how they were resolved. Anton Wiklund reviews every deck in full before it is released.
2. 1. IAU star names: the IAU Working Group on Star Names (WGSN) publishes its IAU Catalog of Star Names (IAU-CSN). The plain-text edition, IAU-CSN.txt (header: “Last updated 2022-04-04”), was downloaded from the WGSN secretary's page at the University of Rochester (query 1). It gives, for every approved name, the star's designation, Bayer letter, constellation abbreviation (Con), component, V magnitude, HIP number and date of adoption, and states that IAU-produced products are released under Creative Commons Attribution. The IAU's own former page (https://www.iau.org/public/themes/naming_stars/) answered 404; the IAU's announcement “New Star Names 2026” (12 February 2026) links to the living catalogue on the WGSN's site exopla.net, which was downloaded (query 2) and its table (640 names, the latest adopted 2026/09/22) parsed (parse_csn.py). Every name brighter than magnitude 2.6 in either table was compared: the current catalogue adds no name for a star brighter than 2.0 (its newer bright names, Uridim, Tiansi and Leepwal, are α Lupi 2.29, γ Cassiopeiae 2.39 and ζ Centauri 2.55), and every name of the deck is in both with the same Bayer letter and constellation.
3. 2. Ranking: the two WGSN tables give different magnitudes for some multiple stars, because the 2022 file gives the magnitude of the named component (Castor 1.98, Shaula 2.08, Acrux 1.33, Algieba 2.61) and the current catalogue mostly the combined light (1.58, 1.63, 0.76, 1.98). The deck ranks by one stated catalogue: the V-band apparent magnitude (P1215 with qualifier P1227 = V band, Q4892529, preferred rank) on the Wikidata item that carries the IAU name, whatever that item models (a system for Castor and Shaula, the named component for Acrux and Rigil Kentaurus). Wikidata items were found from the HIP numbers of both tables (query 3, compare.py), their labels, aliases, constellations (P59) and magnitudes read with wbgetentities (query 5, entities.py), names.py made a first cut on the items found by HIP number (rule in step 6), and the item for each name was then chosen as the one that has the name as an English or multilingual label or alias and a P59 statement (for Sirius the system item Q3409 rather than the Sirius A item that carries the HIP number; for Acrux the α¹ Crucis item Q66476660; for Fomalhaut Q13169, found with wbsearchentities). Where more than one item carries the name, the one with the WGSN file's HIP number is taken (added in review round 4, query 16): this keeps the items already chosen for Aldebaran (Q12170, not the system item Q88540091), Alnitak (Q13076, not ζ Orionis A Q66477108), Hadar (Q13175, not β Centauri A Q66476662), Regulus (Q13013, not Q76493786), Rigil Kentaurus and Toliman (Q2090157 and Q1052548, not the system Q12176) and Shaula (Q13023, not Q78603928), none of which changes a star's side of the 2.0 limit, and gives Q66477100 for Algieba (HIP 50583), not the γ¹ Leonis item Q14203. Where that item has no V-band magnitude (Fomalhaut and Alsephina), the 2022 WGSN file's magnitude is used (1.17 and 1.99). The values equal SIMBAD's V magnitudes (query 9) except Hadar (Wikidata 0.60, SIMBAD 0.58) and Sargas (1.862, 1.85); SIMBAD gives no V for the objects named Acrux (“* alf Cru”, whose component “* alf01 Cru” has 1.28 in query 10) and Alsephina (“* del01 Vel”). In review round 1 the rule was re-applied to the chosen items and to Algieba's item (Q66477100) against live Wikidata (query 15, rule_check.py): all 47 stars then in the deck are below 2.0, Polaris 2.02, Algieba 2.37. In review round 4 Algieba's 2.37 (referenced to UCAC4, an astrometric catalogue) was found to be impossible for the pair, which cannot be fainter than its brighter star γ¹ Leonis (SIMBAD V 2.23, query 16); it was replaced by the preferred V-band value of Q14203, the γ¹ Leonis item that also carries the name (1.98, referenced to Ducati 2002, Johnson photometry), which the current IAU catalogue confirms for the pair (1.98), and Algieba was added as the 48th star. A query for every name of either WGSN table brighter than 2.6 (query 17, all_name_items.py) found Algieba to be the only name outside the deck carried by any Wikidata item with a V-band value below 2.0.
4. 3. Constellations: the constellation of each star is Wikidata's P59. It was compared with the WGSN file's and the current catalogue's Con column, the abbreviation (P1813) of the Wikidata constellation item, and an independent computation: the star's SIMBAD position (ICRS, J2000) placed in the IAU constellation boundaries with astropy's get_constellation (query 11, constellation_check.py; recorded as the source “astropy”). All five agree for every star (the script make_dossier.py asserts it). The English back of each card gives the constellation's English Wikidata label, which is its official Latin name as listed by the IAU's page “The Constellations” (query 8; checked by make_dossier.py), and its Swedish Wikidata label, the same Swedish names as the library's Constellations deck. English uses these IAU (Latin) names as its ordinary names for the constellations, so the English back is tagged “en”; the library's Constellations deck, which asks for the English translations (“Great Dog”), tags the same Latin names “la” on its fronts. Each reader sees one side: English readers the IAU name, Swedish readers the Swedish name.
5. 4. Swedish: the Swedish names of the stars are the IAU names, which Swedish uses unchanged, except Polaris, whose established Swedish name is Polstjärnan (Wikidata sv label; title of the Swedish Wikipedia article). For every star the Swedish Wikipedia article was fetched through the MediaWiki API with its revision id (query 12, svwiki.py; Algieba's in query 16), following redirects and choosing the star article where the name leads to a disambiguation page (Vega, Hadar → Beta Centauri, Pollux, Mimosa, Castor, Atria, Peacock, Polaris → Polstjärnan; Rigil Kentaurus → Alfa Centauri). The lead of each article names the star by the IAU name (or, for Hadar, Miaplacidus and Avior, gives it beside the Bayer name used as the title) and, except Capella, the constellation in Swedish; sv_clauses.py picked the sentence naming the constellation, quoted in each card's evidence. Toliman has no Swedish article; its Swedish name rests on Wikidata's multilingual label and the IAU. Popular Swedish names such as hundstjärnan (Sirius) and Axet (Spica) are not used: only Polstjärnan is established enough to replace the IAU name.
6. 5. Notes: the back note gives the star's Bayer designation, built from the WGSN file's Bayer letter and the constellation's genitive in the IAU's table “The Constellations” (e.g. α + Canis Majoris), with the component for the two stars of the Alpha Centauri pair (WGSN components A and B) and, since review round 4, for Acrux (α¹ Crucis, the item ranked) and Algieba (γ¹ Leonis, the WGSN file's ID “γ1”), each called the brighter star of its pair. Three further cards ask for the brightest and second-brightest star of the night sky (Sirius and Canopus, from the V magnitudes of Wikidata, SIMBAD and the WGSN file and the Swedish Wikipedia) and for the bright star nearest the north celestial pole (Polaris, SIMBAD declination +89.264109° for J2000, 0.736° from the pole; moved to 4 October 2026 with its SIMBAD proper motion, parallax and radial velocity and precessed to the equinox of that date with astropy, 0.626°; closest, 0.46°, in 2102 in a yearly sampling of 2000–2200; query 15, polaris_today.py). Study direction: front to back only, since several stars share a constellation.
7. 6. Evidence and machine checks: make_dossier.py (query 14) wrote the cards and the evidence of every star card from the saved, parsed files (the WGSN file, the current catalogue, the Wikidata entities, the IAU constellations table, the SIMBAD results, the astropy computation and the Swedish Wikipedia leads), so that every “says” is what the parsed source holds; the evidence of the three superlative cards was written by hand from the same files. The scripts are not published with the deck; their rules are: parse_csn.py reads the largest HTML table of the catalogue page into rows keyed by its header (a repeated header row at the end is not a name). make_q3.py collects the HIP numbers of every row below magnitude 2.6 in either WGSN table. compare.py joins the q3 results to both tables by HIP number. names.py (the first cut) keeps every name of the 2022 WGSN file whose HIP-matched Wikidata item has a V-band magnitude below 2.0 (the preferred-rank value, else any value; where there is none, the WGSN file's magnitude), plus Polaris; stars.py then fixes the item carrying each name (step 2). make_dossier.py takes each item's magnitude as the first preferred-rank, non-deprecated P1215 value with P1227 = Q4892529, else the first non-deprecated one, else the WGSN file's value, sorts by it, and asserts for every star that the item has exactly one IAU constellation in P59 and that its P1813 abbreviation equals the WGSN Con, the current catalogue's Constellation and astropy's short name, and that the IAU table's name equals the Wikidata en label. constellation_check.py calls get_constellation(SkyCoord(ra * u.deg, dec * u.deg, frame='icrs')) and get_constellation(…, short_name=True) on the positions of simbad-names.csv. entities.py, fetch_cons.py and svwiki.py make the GET requests recorded in queries 5, 6 and 12, in batches (50 items; 20 titles), and sv_clauses.py picks the sentence of each Swedish lead that names the constellation. For every star card the builder checks against live Wikidata that the star item has the constellation as P59, has the English and Swedish front as a label or alias (in that language or mul), has the V magnitude used for the ranking as a P1215 value (where Wikidata has one), and that the constellation item has the English and Swedish back as labels. The built deck was validated with the app's SHACL and DCAT-AP validators (validate_sources.ts).

## Selection

Every star with an IAU-approved proper name (IAU Catalog of Star Names) whose V-band apparent magnitude is below 2.0, as of 4 October 2026: 48 stars, from Sirius (−1.46) to Alsephina (1.99). The magnitude is the preferred V-band value on the Wikidata item that carries the IAU name as an English or multilingual label or alias and has a constellation (P59); where several items carry the name (Aldebaran, Alnitak, Hadar, Regulus, Rigil Kentaurus, Shaula, Toliman, Algieba), the one that has the star's HIP number from the WGSN file; where that item has no V-band value (Fomalhaut, Alsephina), the WGSN file's value. The rule takes the value of whatever that item models: the combined light where the item is the system (Castor 1.58, Shaula 1.63), the named component's light where it is the component (Acrux 1.28, Rigil Kentaurus 0.01). One value is replaced: Algieba's item (Q66477100, the γ Leonis pair, HIP 50583) has the preferred V-band value 2.37 (from the UCAC4 astrometric catalogue), which cannot be the pair's light, since its brighter star γ¹ Leonis alone is 2.23 in SIMBAD; the deck uses instead the preferred V-band value of the other item that carries the name Algieba, the γ¹ Leonis item Q14203 (1.98, from Johnson photometry of the unresolved pair), which the current IAU catalogue confirms for the pair (1.98). Algieba stays a borderline case: the Swedish Wikipedia gives the pair 2.08, and the 2022 WGSN file gives γ¹ Leonis alone 2.61. In effect, for the borderline multiple stars (Castor, Shaula, Algieba) the deck ranks by the combined light that the eye sees as one point: Algieba is in the deck on the light of the unresolved pair, and its IAU-named star γ¹ Leonis alone would be fainter than 2.0 (2.23 in SIMBAD). Polaris (2.02) is added as the 49th star, as the pole star, together with three cards on undisputed superlatives (the brightest and the second-brightest star of the night sky, and the star nearest the north celestial pole): 52 cards. Left out: the Sun; stars brighter than 2.0 that have no IAU name (γ² Velorum, 1.83; α² Crucis, 1.58, the companion of Acrux); stars just fainter than 2.0 (Hamal and Diphda 2.01); galaxies and other non-stellar objects. The 2.0 limit is the deck's own round cut-off: magnitudes near it differ by a few hundredths between catalogues, and the selection follows the stated rule rather than any list of brightest stars. In Swedish the stars keep their IAU names, except Polaris, whose established Swedish name Polstjärnan is used; popular names such as hundstjärnan (Sirius) and Axet (Spica) are not.

}

**9. SIMBAD main identifier, position, V magnitude and NAME identifiers of every star, by HIP number (simbad.adql, written by make_simbad.py) and by name (simbad-names.adql)** (SIMBAD astronomical database)

```
python3 <scratch>/make_simbad.py
curl -s -A "solid-memo deck research (https://github.com/antwika/solid-memo)" --data-urlencode "request=doQuery" --data-urlencode "lang=adql" --data-urlencode "format=csv" --data-urlencode query@<scratch>/simbad.adql -o <scratch>/simbad.csv https://simbad.cds.unistra.fr/simbad/sim-tap/sync
curl -s -A "solid-memo deck research (https://github.com/antwika/solid-memo)" --data-urlencode "request=doQuery" --data-urlencode "lang=adql" --data-urlencode "format=csv" --data-urlencode query@<scratch>/simbad-names.adql -o <scratch>/simbad-names.csv https://simbad.cds.unistra.fr/simbad/sim-tap/sync

simbad.adql:
SELECT h.id AS hip, b.main_id, b.ra, b.dec, f.V, n.id AS name
FROM ident AS h
JOIN basic AS b ON b.oid = h.oidref
LEFT JOIN allfluxes AS f ON f.oidref = b.oid
LEFT JOIN ident AS n ON n.oidref = b.oid AND n.id LIKE 'NAME %'
WHERE h.id IN ('HIP 32349', 'HIP 30438', 'HIP 69673', 'HIP 71683', 'HIP 91262', 'HIP 24608', 'HIP 24436', 'HIP 37279', 'HIP 27989', 'HIP 7588', 'HIP 68702', 'HIP 97649', 'HIP 60718', 'HIP 21421', 'HIP 80763', 'HIP 65474', 'HIP 37826', 'HIP 113368', 'HIP 62434', 'HIP 102098', 'HIP 71681', 'HIP 49669', 'HIP 33579', 'HIP 36850', 'HIP 85927', 'HIP 61084', 'HIP 25336', 'HIP 25428', 'HIP 45238', 'HIP 26311', 'HIP 109268', 'HIP 26727', 'HIP 62956', 'HIP 15863', 'HIP 54061', 'HIP 90185', 'HIP 34444', 'HIP 86228', 'HIP 67301', 'HIP 41037', 'HIP 82273', 'HIP 28360', 'HIP 100751', 'HIP 31681', 'HIP 30324', 'HIP 46390', 'HIP 42913', 'HIP 11767')

simbad-names.adql:
SELECT n.id AS name, b.main_id, b.ra, b.dec, f.V
FROM ident AS n
JOIN basic AS b ON b.oid = n.oidref
LEFT JOIN allfluxes AS f ON f.oidref = b.oid
WHERE n.id IN ('NAME Sirius', 'NAME Canopus', 'NAME Arcturus', 'NAME Rigil Kentaurus', 'NAME Vega', 'NAME Capella', 'NAME Rigel', 'NAME Procyon', 'NAME Betelgeuse', 'NAME Achernar', 'NAME Hadar', 'NAME Altair', 'NAME Acrux', 'NAME Aldebaran', 'NAME Antares', 'NAME Spica', 'NAME Pollux', 'NAME Fomalhaut', 'NAME Mimosa', 'NAME Deneb', 'NAME Toliman', 'NAME Regulus', 'NAME Adhara', 'NAME Castor', 'NAME Shaula', 'NAME Gacrux', 'NAME Bellatrix', 'NAME Elnath', 'NAME Miaplacidus', 'NAME Alnilam', 'NAME Alnair', 'NAME Alnitak', 'NAME Alioth', 'NAME Mirfak', 'NAME Dubhe', 'NAME Kaus Australis', 'NAME Wezen', 'NAME Sargas', 'NAME Alkaid', 'NAME Avior', 'NAME Atria', 'NAME Menkalinan', 'NAME Peacock', 'NAME Alhena', 'NAME Mirzam', 'NAME Alphard', 'NAME Alsephina', 'NAME Polaris')
```

**10. Every SIMBAD object brighter than V 2.0, to find bright stars without an IAU name and to check the superlatives (the first attempt, with the alias V in ORDER BY, was refused by the ADQL parser)** (SIMBAD astronomical database)

```

simbad-bright.adql:
SELECT b.main_id, f.V AS vmag, b.otype
FROM basic AS b
JOIN allfluxes AS f ON f.oidref = b.oid
WHERE f.V < 2.0
ORDER BY vmag
```

## Quality control

7 rounds, 26 findings: 19 fixed, 0 rejected after checking, 7 needing no change. Every card's Wikidata checks (301 in all) are re-run against live Wikidata by `scripts/authored_decks.py check` before every build.

### Round 0: Sources, licences and machine checks: every star's IAU name against both WGSN tables and SIMBAD; its constellation against Wikidata P59, both WGSN tables, the Wikidata abbreviation and an astropy computation from the SIMBAD position; its magnitude against Wikidata, SIMBAD and both WGSN tables; the Swedish names against Wikidata sv labels and the Swedish Wikipedia. (2026-10-04)

**Reviewer:** Claude (AI) — authoring agent, machine checks · **Scope:** All 51 cards, the selection, the sources and the deck metadata.

All 48 names are in both WGSN tables and in SIMBAD (as NAME identifiers); for every star the five constellation readings agree; the Wikidata V magnitudes equal SIMBAD's except two that differ by 0.02 or less (Hadar, Sargas), which does not move either across the 2.0 limit. No Wikidata check was skipped. The findings concern differences between catalogues that shaped the selection, Wikidata modelling and a few errors in the Swedish Wikipedia that do not reach the cards.

**Reviewer:** Claude (AI) — independent Factual accuracy reviewer · **Scope:** All 51 cards, the selection and the method, re-checked against SIMBAD TAP, the current IAU catalogue on exopla.net and live Wikidata.

The reviewer re-checked every star's V magnitude in SIMBAD, re-downloaded the current IAU catalogue, ran every Wikidata check and found the facts on all 51 cards correct; round 0 reproduced. Two warnings (the pole-star note gave the J2000 distance for a front that says “today”; the selection's “combined light” wording did not match its rule) and one suggestion (the catalogue row count) were raised. Both warnings were confirmed and fixed; the row count was corrected to 640, which is what the parse produces, not the reviewer's 647.

| Card | Issue | Resolution | Outcome |
|---|---|---|---|
| north-pole-star | The back note “Declination +89.26° (J2000): about 0.7° from the pole” gives the J2000 distance (0.736°), but the front asks for the pole star today; with precession and proper motion Polaris is about 0.63° from the pole in 2026. | Confirmed: SIMBAD's J2000 position, proper motion (44.48, −11.85 mas/yr), parallax and radial velocity, moved to 2026-10-04 and precessed to FK5 of date with astropy, give 0.626° (0.736° at J2000; closest, 0.46°, in 2102). The note now reads “About 0.6° from the pole in 2026 (0.74° in 2000); it will come closest around 2100.” / “Omkring 0,6° från polen år 2026 (0,74° år 2000); den kommer närmast omkring år 2100.”; the computation is query 15 and an astropy evidence entry on the card. | fixed |
| deck | The selection says the rule “follows the combined light of close multiple stars that appear as one point to the eye (Castor, Shaula)”, but Acrux and Rigil Kentaurus are ranked on component values and Algieba, a close pair of combined light 1.98, is excluded; the real rule is the V value on the Wikidata item that carries the name. | Confirmed and reworded: the selection and method step 2 now say the rule takes the preferred V-band value of whatever the name-carrying item models (system for Castor 1.58 and Shaula 1.63, component for Acrux 1.28 and Rigil Kentaurus 0.01), and state Algieba's exclusion as a borderline consequence. One correction to the suggested wording: Algieba's item Q66477100 is not the component item; it is labelled “Gamma Leonis” (mul “Algieba”) with aliases for the pair (“ADS 7724 AB”, HD 89484 and HD 89485), and its preferred V 2.37 matches neither the combined 1.98 (current IAU catalogue) nor γ¹'s 2.23 (SIMBAD, checked; SIMBAD has no V for “* gam Leo”), so the selection describes it as the pair's item. The rule was re-applied to live Wikidata for all chosen items and Algieba's (rule_check.py, query 15): the same 47 stars, Polaris 2.02, Algieba 2.37. Method step 6 now also states that names.py's first cut used the HIP-matched items. | fixed |

### Round 4: Re-check of changed cards and a sample (facts, language, documentation) (2026-10-04)

**Reviewer:** Claude (AI) — independent re-check reviewer · **Scope:** All 51 cards re-checked against live Wikidata, SIMBAD, the current IAU catalogue on exopla.net, astropy and the Swedish Wikipedia; the built deck, the description, the method, the licensing and the quality-control log.

The reviewer confirmed every card, every Wikidata check and every fix of rounds 1–3, and raised one error and one suggestion. The error was confirmed and went further than reported: the stated rule did not settle which item to use for eight names carried by more than one Wikidata item, and for Algieba the choice decided the selection. A tie-break by HIP number was added, which keeps every earlier choice; Algieba's V value on that item (2.37) was shown to be impossible and replaced by the 1.98 of the other item carrying the name, confirmed by the current IAU catalogue, so Algieba was added: 49 stars, 52 cards. The suggestion on Acrux's note was applied.

| Card | Issue | Resolution | Outcome |
|---|---|---|---|
| deck | The rule takes the magnitude from the item that has the name as an en/mul label or alias and a P59, but two items fit for Algieba: the pair item Q66477100 (V 2.37), the only one the dossier names, and the γ¹ Leonis item Q14203 (en/mul alias “Algieba”, P59 Leo, preferred V 1.98). By the Acrux precedent (component item) Algieba would be in the deck; the selection, method and earlier rounds present it as excluded by the rule. | Confirmed (query 16): Q14203 carries the alias “Algieba” in en and mul, P59 Q8853 and a preferred V-band value 1.98; its latest revision is of 2026-03-18. A query for every deck name (query 16) showed the same ambiguity for seven more names (Aldebaran, Alnitak, Hadar, Regulus, Rigil Kentaurus, Shaula, Toliman), so the Acrux precedent is not a rule: the deck uses the system item for Hadar and the component item for Regulus. The tie-break “the item with the WGSN file's HIP number” was added to the selection and method step 2; it keeps every item chosen before and gives Q66477100 (P528 HIP 50583; also the current IAU catalogue's HIP and SIMBAD object “* gam Leo” for Algieba) for Algieba. That item's preferred V 2.37 is referenced to UCAC4, an astrometric catalogue, and is fainter than γ¹ Leonis alone (SIMBAD V 2.23), which a pair cannot be, so it was set aside, as the deck's policy is to keep the better-sourced value: the deck uses Q14203's preferred V 1.98 (Ducati 2002, Johnson photometry), which the current IAU catalogue confirms for the pair (1.98), so the value comes from CC0 Wikidata and the catalogue stays a verification source. Algieba is therefore below 2.0 and was added as a card (back Leo / Lejonet; note γ¹ Leonis; checks P59 and labels on Q66477100 and P1215 1.98 on Q14203, no P1215 check on Q66477100). The Swedish Wikipedia's combined 2.08 and the WGSN file's γ¹ 2.61 are named in the selection, which calls Algieba borderline. Query 17 found no other name of either WGSN table brighter than 2.6 outside the deck with any Wikidata item below 2.0. Description (49 stars, 52 cards), selection and method steps 2, 4 and 5 updated; rounds 0 and 1 are left as they were logged. | fixed |
| acrux | The Bayer notes name components inconsistently: Rigil Kentaurus and Toliman give α Centauri A / B, but Acrux, ranked on its α¹ Crucis item (V 1.28), says only “α Crucis”. | Confirmed: the ranked item Q66476660 is α¹ Crucis and the WGSN gives component “Aa” (of α¹). The note now reads “Bayer designation: α¹ Crucis, the brighter star of the Alpha Crucis pair.” / “Bayerbeteckning: α¹ Crucis, den ljusare stjärnan i paret Alfa Crucis.” The new Algieba card follows the same pattern (γ¹ Leonis), and method step 5 says so. | fixed |
